Part 1 — Not All That Wheezes Is Asthma: Differential Diagnosis

What is wheezing?

Wheezing is a high-pitched, musical sound produced when air is forced through narrow airways. When obstruction is severe, wheezing can be heard on both inspiration and expiration (not just expiration). It is often associated with labored breathing — retractions, nasal flaring, and decreased ability to speak in full sentences.

In asthma specifically, wheeze results from three processes: mucus plugging, inflammation in the small airways, and reversible bronchoconstriction.

Clinical pearlNot all that wheezes is asthma — wheeze is a final common sound produced by airway narrowing from many different causes, acute and chronic. The job of the history and exam is to sort out which one.

Differential diagnosis of wheezing

Acute wheezeChronic or recurrent wheeze
Asthma (exacerbation)Asthma
BronchiolitisGERD
Atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma pneumoniae)Cystic fibrosis
Foreign body aspirationPrimary ciliary dyskinesia
AnaphylaxisVocal cord dysfunction (inducible laryngeal obstruction)
—Structural causes (vascular rings, tracheal stenosis, mediastinal mass)

Table 1 — Differential diagnosis of asthma by age and characteristic findings

Table 1 (part 1): bronchiolitis, viral-induced wheeze, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, chronic aspiration/GERD, tracheomalacia/bronchomalacia, bronchiectasis, food allergy, anxiety/panic attack, and vocal cord dysfunction — age, distinguishing findings, and diagnostic tests
Table 1 (part 2): vocal cord dysfunction, heart failure, foreign body aspiration, mass effect, underlying immunodeficiency, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and cystic fibrosis — age, distinguishing findings, and diagnostic tests. (Patel & Teach, Pediatr Rev 2019;40(11):549-567)

Pertinent history questions

Narrowing the differential starts with more history. Ask whether the child has:

  • Wheezed before?
  • Ever been hospitalized for a breathing-related issue (pneumonia, RSV, bronchiolitis, asthma)?
  • Used an inhaler before — and if so, did it help?
  • Other symptoms: cold symptoms, allergic symptoms, a choking event?
  • A history of prematurity and oxygen need?
  • A history of congenital heart disease or murmurs?
  • A family history of asthma, eczema, or atopy?

Case 1 — the wheezing infant

CaseHealthy 6-month-old presents with 3 days of rhinorrhea and cough. It is November and the child attends daycare. Today the patient is working harder to breathe, is wheezing, and feels warm to touch. Never wheezed before, never hospitalized, born full term without a NICU stay, no medications or allergies, no tobacco exposure, no history of eczema.

PE: T 100.6°F, RR 42, HR 146, SpO2 96%. General: well-appearing, no distress. HEENT: nares congested with clear discharge, no flaring. Resp: mild subcostal retractions, equal bilateral air movement with scattered rhonchi and wheezing. CV/GI/skin: normal.

Working through the options

OptionWhy it fits or doesn't
Asthma exacerbationUnlikely — age <2, and this is the first-ever episode of wheezing. (If viral-induced wheezing continues into future illnesses, a diagnosis of asthma may eventually be made.)
GERDHistory doesn't mention recurrent spit-up, acid-reflux medications, or a choking episode before symptoms started
PneumoniaPossible given fever/cold symptoms/mild increased work of breathing, but community-acquired pneumonia typically shows acute fever, worsening cough, and decreased air movement with crackles focal to the lobar site — diagnosed clinically ± CXR, treated with antibiotics
Congestive heart failureUnlikely — normal cardiac exam, no hepatomegaly, no history of congenital heart disease
Viral-induced wheezing / bronchiolitisCorrect. Bronchiolitis is a lower respiratory tract infection in children <2 years old with lower-respiratory symptoms and wheezing, commonly caused by RSV (though many viruses can cause it)
Clinical pearlRSV bronchiolitis has been associated with an increased rate of wheezing with future viral illnesses and, eventually, a diagnosis of asthma. Bronchiolitis is typically supportive care — nasal suctioning, smaller and more frequent feeds — and typically does not respond to SABA (albuterol). Hospitalize with supplemental oxygen if hypoxemic (SpO2 <90%).

Case 2 — the teenage soccer player

Case14-year-old female soccer player presents with concerns for difficulty breathing during sports participation. Never diagnosed with asthma, but tried a friend's albuterol inhaler at practice and it didn't help. Shortness of breath occurs with games, not practices. Sometimes feels like she 'can't get a breath in' with a loud wheezing sound. No nighttime cough, allergies, wheezing with colds, eczema, or family history of asthma.

PE: T 98.6°F, RR 14, HR 90, SpO2 100%, BP 115/78. Fully normal exam — clear lungs, normal I:E ratio, no wheeze/rales/rhonchi/accessory muscle use, no clubbing.

Working through the options

OptionWhy it fits or doesn't
AsthmaUnlikely — symptoms don't occur outside of games, and albuterol does not help her symptoms
GERDHistory doesn't mention heartburn, making this diagnosis less likely
Exercise-induced asthmaPossible — symptoms recur with sports — but only during games (not practices), and it does not respond to albuterol. True asthma should improve with SABA use.
Vocal cord dysfunctionCorrect — see below
Cystic fibrosisUnlikely — no history of recurrent sinusitis/respiratory illness, poor growth, or exam findings such as nasal polyps or digital clubbing

Vocal cord dysfunction (inducible laryngeal obstruction)

VCD is the paradoxical/inappropriate adduction (closure) of the vocal cords during the inspiratory phase of respiration. Closure produces partial to severe obstruction of airflow. It is a functional disorder that serves as a classic asthma mimicker, often triggered by high-stress situations (competitive games, not low-stress practices). Symptoms are periodic, can provoke fear/panic/anxiety that further worsens respiratory symptoms, and are refractory to SABA and inhaled corticosteroids. Auscultation during an acute episode may reveal stridor (an upper-airway, inspiratory sound) rather than wheeze.

Flexible laryngoscopy — the gold standard for diagnosis. A: paradoxical adduction of the vocal cords during inspiration. B: appropriate vocal cord movement for comparison.

Diagnosis: clinically, with a good history and exam; PFTs can be considered; gold standard is direct visualization via flexible laryngoscopy.
Treatment: speech therapy exercises to help the patient learn to relax the vocal cords; consider treating underlying anxiety if present.

Case 3 — back to a classic asthma exacerbation

Case6-year-old presents with wheezing. Woke up today with coughing, increased work of breathing, and wheezing, but has had a runny nose and cough for a couple of days. History of wheezing with colds in the past, possibly needing an inhaler as a toddler during those colds (1-2 prior episodes). FHx: childhood asthma (mom). PMH: never hospitalized, no known allergies, no medications, + eczema.

PE: T 99.1°F, RR 34, HR 140, SpO2 91%. General: alert, appears scared, mild respiratory distress. HEENT: nares congested with clear discharge, no flare. Resp: mild subcostal retractions, decreased bilateral air movement with prolonged exhalation and diffuse expiratory wheezing, + tachypnea. CV: tachycardic, regular rhythm, no murmur. GI/skin: normal.

Working through the options (asthma exacerbation, vocal cord dysfunction, pneumonia, congestive heart failure, foreign body) — vocal cord dysfunction is more common in the teenage years with difficulty on inspiration, often with stridor; pneumonia is possible but there's no fever and focal findings would be expected after a nebulizer treatment; CHF is unlikely with no history of congenital heart disease, murmur, crackles, or hepatomegaly; foreign body is possible but there's no report of choking/playing with a small object, and it tends to produce asymmetric lung findings.

Correct answer: asthma exacerbation. This patient has a history of recurrent wheezing and prior albuterol use, plus history/exam suggestive of a viral URI — a common asthma trigger. Classic exam findings in asthma: prolonged exhalation (increased I:E ratio) and expiratory wheezing; depending on severity of obstruction, respiratory distress (nasal flaring, retractions); can develop hypoxemia (saturations <90%). The next step is a SABA (albuterol) nebulizer — management is covered fully in Part 2.

Reference — normal vital signs in pediatric patients

Pediatric normal ranges shift substantially with age — a heart rate or respiratory rate that would be alarming in an adult can be entirely normal in a neonate or infant. Keep this chart handy when assessing any pediatric patient with respiratory symptoms.

Normal heart rates, respiratory rates, and blood pressures in children, from neonate through adolescent (Hazinski MF, Nursing Care of the Critically Ill Child, 3rd ed.)

Part 1 practice questions

Exam-style question
A previously healthy 7-month-old in November, who attends daycare, presents with 3 days of rhinorrhea/cough followed by tachypnea, wheezing, and low-grade fever. This is her first episode of wheezing ever. Exam shows mild subcostal retractions and scattered rhonchi/wheeze bilaterally, SpO2 96%. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
AAsthma exacerbation
BVocal cord dysfunction
CViral-induced wheezing/bronchiolitis
DCongestive heart failure
EGERD
Explanation: A first episode of wheezing in an infant <2 years old, in the context of a viral URI (often RSV, peak season fall/winter), is classic bronchiolitis — a clinical diagnosis that typically does not respond to SABA and is managed supportively.
Exam-style question
Which finding would make an asthma exacerbation LESS likely as the cause of a 6-month-old's first wheezing episode?
AA family history of asthma
BThe presence of a viral prodrome
CThe presence of subcostal retractions
DA low-grade fever
EAge under 2 years with no prior wheezing history
Explanation: Asthma is a diagnosis of recurrent, reversible airway obstruction; a true first episode of wheeze at this young age, with no prior history, argues against an asthma exacerbation, favoring viral-induced wheeze/bronchiolitis instead.
Exam-style question
A 15-year-old competitive swimmer develops episodic shortness of breath and a loud wheezing sound only during high-stakes meets, not during practice. Symptoms do not improve with albuterol. Flexible laryngoscopy during a symptomatic episode shows paradoxical adduction of the vocal cords during inspiration. What is the diagnosis?
AExercise-induced bronchoconstriction
BVocal cord dysfunction (inducible laryngeal obstruction)
CForeign body aspiration
DBronchiectasis
EAllergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
Explanation: Paradoxical vocal cord adduction on inspiration, refractory to SABA, and situational triggering by high-stress performance rather than exertion alone, is the classic picture of vocal cord dysfunction — a well-known asthma mimicker.
Exam-style question
Which treatment is most appropriate for vocal cord dysfunction?
AHigh-dose inhaled corticosteroids
BDaily montelukast
CEmergent bronchoscopy for foreign body removal
DSpeech therapy exercises ± treatment of underlying anxiety
EBack-to-back albuterol nebulizer treatments
Explanation: VCD does not respond to asthma medications (SABA/ICS). Treatment centers on speech therapy techniques to relax the vocal cords, along with addressing any underlying anxiety.
Exam-style question
A 6-year-old with a history of eczema and a mother with childhood asthma presents with 2 days of URI symptoms followed by wheezing, tachypnea, and SpO2 91%. Exam shows decreased air movement with prolonged exhalation and diffuse expiratory wheeze. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?
ASABA (albuterol) nebulizer treatment
BIpratropium alone
CReassurance and observation only
DEmpiric antibiotics for pneumonia
EImmediate flexible laryngoscopy
Explanation: This is a classic asthma exacerbation triggered by a viral URI in a child with atopic risk factors (eczema, maternal asthma, prior wheezing episodes). The first step in management is a SABA nebulizer treatment.

Part 2 — Asthma Evaluation & Management

Asthma — overview and risk factors

Asthma is a disorder of restricted airflow due to inflammation, bronchoconstriction, and mucus production/plugging. It is a significant health problem worldwide (especially in resource-rich countries) and is one of the most common chronic diseases of childhood — an estimated 5.5 million children in the US carry this diagnosis. Establishing a diagnosis involves history taking, physical exam, and diagnostic studies.

Risk factors

  • A child with one asthmatic parent is 2.6x more likely to have asthma
  • Children with a history of eczema and allergies (atopic children)

Asthma Predictive Index (API)

In patients under age 3 who have had 3 or more episodes of wheezing in a year, AND either (1) a parent with asthma or the patient has eczema, OR (2) the patient has allergic rhinitis, wheezing without URIs, or an eosinophil count >4% (2 of these) — the API is positive.

Clinical pearlA positive Asthma Predictive Index makes the likelihood of developing chronic asthma 4-7 times more likely than in children who don't meet these criteria.

How does asthma present?

  • Chronic cough >3 weeks
  • Prolonged cough after acute URIs
  • Wheezing with viral illnesses
  • Shortness of breath/cough with exercise or sport
  • Can present with chest tightness, shortness of breath, chest pain
  • Can be associated with eczema, allergy history

Diagnosing asthma — evaluate for symptoms first

Coughing + wheezing are the most common symptoms of childhood asthma. Other symptoms: breathlessness, chest tightness, chest pain.

SymptomClassic character
CoughNocturnal, recurs seasonally, or triggered by cold air/exercise/allergens; lasting >3 weeks (especially after a URI); typically dry and hacking
WheezeConsidered the hallmark of childhood asthma (though sometimes absent — cough may be the only symptom); high-pitched, musical, polyphonic (varied pitch); classically expiratory, but can be both inspiratory and expiratory if severe narrowing

How do you diagnose asthma?

<5 years old≥5 years old
Spirometry cannot be performedHistory + physical suggestive
A trial of asthma medications may help establish the diagnosisSpirometry pre- and post-albuterol → demonstration of reversible airflow obstruction establishes the diagnosis
Reversal of symptoms with albuterol suggests asthmaPreferred method of diagnosis in patients ≥5 years if asthma is suspected

Spirometry

Normal flow-volume loop: expiration above the axis, inspiration below. FVC = forced vital capacity; FEV1 = forced expiratory volume in the first second.

FVC = forced vital capacity. FEV1 = forced expiratory volume in the first second. Airflow obstruction = FEV1 <80% predicted AND FEV1/FVC ratio <0.85 (85%). Perform spirometry pre- and post-SABA to assess for reversibility; an increase in FEV1 by >10-12% after bronchodilator is considered significant/reversible.

Worked example — obstructive defect on spirometry in a 9-year-old

Pre-bronchodilator FEV1 65% (FEV1/FVC 66) improves to post-bronchodilator FEV1 93% (FEV1/FVC 79) — a 44% improvement, well above the 10% significance threshold, confirming reversible airflow obstruction.
Clinical pearlRemember: an increase in FEV1 of at least 10% after bronchodilator is considered significant reversibility and establishes the diagnosis of asthma in a patient ≥5 years old.

Asthma classification

Severity is classified along two axes: impairment (how often do symptoms occur?) and risk (how severe are the episodes?). Assign severity to the most severe category in which any feature occurs.

NAEPP classification of asthma severity in children 5-11 years: symptoms, nighttime awakenings, SABA use, activity interference, and lung function (impairment), plus exacerbations requiring oral steroids (risk)
CategoryDaytime symptomsNocturnal awakeningsActivity interferenceExacerbations/yr
Intermittent≤2 days/wk≤2 nights/moNone≤1
Mild persistent>2 but <7 days/wk3-4 nights/moMild>2
Moderate persistentDaily>1/week but not dailySome limitation>2
Severe persistentThroughout the dayMost nightsVery limited>2 (SABA use several times/day)

Treating pediatric asthma patients

Acute managementChronic management
Medications to treat an acute asthma exacerbation — outpatient office, ER, or hospitalLong-term medications to control asthma; managed by pediatricians, pulmonologists, or allergist/immunologists depending on physician comfort and disease severity

Asthma medications

ClassExamples / notes
Short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA)Albuterol
Long-acting beta-2 agonist (LABA)Formoterol
Leukotriene inhibitorMontelukast — black box warning for increased suicidality risk/mood disturbances
Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS)Multiple brands; low/medium/high dose
Systemic steroidsOral and IV
AnticholinergicsIpratropium (Atrovent); ipratropium + albuterol nebulizer (Duoneb — ER use)
Magnesium sulfate (IV)ER/hospital use for severe exacerbations

Step therapy

ClassificationPreferred therapy
Intermittent — Step 1SABA as needed. Alternatives: low-dose ICS whenever SABA used, or short course low-dose ICS at start of a URI
Mild persistent — Step 2Daily low-dose ICS + SABA as needed. Alternative: daily LTRA, or low-dose ICS whenever SABA used
Moderate persistent — Step 3Daily medium-dose ICS, or low-dose ICS-LABA, with SABA as needed. Alternatives: low-dose ICS/ICS-LABA + LTRA; daily and PRN low-dose ICS-LABA
Severe persistent — Step 4Daily medium-dose ICS-LABA with SABA as needed. Alternatives: daily medium-dose ICS + LTRA; daily high-dose ICS; daily and PRN medium-dose ICS-LABA

Standard chronic therapy is daily ICS + PRN SABA, with step-up therapy based on asthma severity and control.

2020 NAEPP focused update — stepwise approach by age

Stepwise approach for asthma management (Steps 1-6) across three age bands: 0-4 years, 5-11 years, and 12+ years — preferred therapy escalates from PRN SABA up through daily high-dose ICS-LABA + oral systemic corticosteroid
Clinical pearlThe step-therapy tables are organized by age band (0-4, 5-11, 12+) because both the preferred medication combinations (e.g., ICS-formoterol options appear starting at age 5) and the highest achievable step differ by age. Know that therapy steps UP with worsening control and steps DOWN once well-controlled for a sustained period.

Assessing asthma control

Classification of asthma control in children 5-11 years: well-controlled, not well-controlled, and very poorly controlled, by symptom frequency, nighttime awakenings, activity interference, SABA use, lung function, and exacerbation history

Level of control is based on the most severe impairment or risk category present. Frequent, intense exacerbations (urgent care, hospitalization, ICU admission) indicate poorer control. Patients with ≥2 exacerbations requiring oral steroids in the past year may be considered the same as patients who are not well-controlled, even without other impairment features.

Exercise-induced asthma

Symptoms occur only with sport/exercise and improve with SABA use prior to activity. Treatment: SABA (albuterol), 2 puffs with a spacer, 15 minutes prior to sport. Patients do not necessarily need to start daily ICS just because they use albuterol every day prior to sport — but if they use SABA at times unassociated with exercise, they may need an ICS.

The Asthma Action Plan

A written plan organized into a familiar traffic-light system that patients and families can follow at home.

Asthma Action Plan: Green Zone (doing well — daily controller medications, pre-exercise SABA), Yellow Zone (asthma getting worse — add quick-relief medicine, consider oral steroid if not improving), Red Zone (medical alert — take quick-relief + oral steroid, call the doctor or go to the ER)
ZoneMeaningAction
GreenDoing well — no cough/wheeze/chest tightness/SOB, normal activityContinue daily controller medications; SABA before exercise if prescribed
YellowAsthma getting worse — cough/wheeze/chest tightness, some activity limitation, nighttime symptomsAdd quick-relief medicine, continue green-zone medicine; if not back to green zone in 1 hour, may need an oral steroid — call the doctor
RedMedical alert — very short of breath, quick-relief medicine not helping, symptoms same/worse after 24h in yellow zoneTake quick-relief medicine + oral steroid; call the doctor now; go to the hospital/call an ambulance for danger signs (trouble walking/talking due to SOB, blue lips/fingernails)

Case — the known asthmatic in exacerbation

Case13-year-old known asthmatic on controller medications presents with a URI for 4 days. Had a fever the first day, but now has worsening cough and feels short of breath. Has been taking her ICS as prescribed and needing albuterol every 4 hours. Meds: fluticasone 44 mcg 2 puffs BID + albuterol 2 puffs q4h prn cough.

PE: T 99.0°F, RR 20, HR 122, BP 120/75, SpO2 90%. General: alert, moderate distress, talking in short sentences. HEENT: nasal congestion, clear rhinorrhea, no pharyngeal erythema. Resp: diffuse wheeze, decreased aeration in the bases posteriorly, using accessory muscles to breathe. Cardiac: tachycardic, regular rhythm, no murmur/rub/gallop. Abdomen: soft, non-tender, non-distended.

This is an asthma exacerbation.

Treatment options

Office:

  • Albuterol nebulizer and check response — can give back-to-back x3, assessing response after each treatment
  • Consider an oral steroid: dexamethasone x1 today and repeat dose tomorrow, or prednisone 2 mg/kg/day divided BID x5 days (max dose 60 mg/day)
  • May need to increase controller medications
  • May need hospitalization if: hypoxemia, or not improving with the above interventions
Clinical pearlThere may be a transient drop in SpO2 immediately after starting an albuterol nebulizer due to a V/Q mismatch (albuterol preferentially vasodilates poorly-ventilated units) — this is expected and does not necessarily mean the treatment is failing.

Part 2 practice questions

Exam-style question
A 9-year-old undergoes spirometry for suspected asthma: pre-bronchodilator FEV1 is 65% predicted (FEV1/FVC 66%); post-bronchodilator FEV1 rises to 93% predicted (FEV1/FVC 79%). What does this represent?
AA non-significant, expected variation
BA restrictive lung defect
CSignificant reversible airflow obstruction, consistent with asthma
DEvidence against a diagnosis of asthma
EAn inadequate bronchodilator response
Explanation: A 44% relative improvement in FEV1 after bronchodilator, well above the 10-12% significance threshold, demonstrates reversible airflow obstruction — the finding that establishes the diagnosis of asthma in a child ≥5 years.
Exam-style question
A 3-year-old has had 4 wheezing episodes this year and has eczema. Her father has asthma. What does a positive Asthma Predictive Index in this child indicate about her future risk?
ANo increased risk of asthma
BA definitive diagnosis of asthma already
CIncreased risk of cystic fibrosis only
DA need for immediate spirometry
EA 4-7 times greater likelihood of developing chronic asthma
Explanation: A positive Asthma Predictive Index (≥3 wheezing episodes/year under age 3, plus a parent with asthma or the child's own eczema, or 2 of allergic rhinitis/wheezing apart from colds/eosinophilia >4%) confers a 4-7x greater likelihood of developing chronic asthma — though spirometry cannot yet be performed at this age.
Exam-style question
A 14-year-old with moderate persistent asthma reports daily daytime symptoms, nocturnal awakenings more than once a week (not nightly), some limitation of activity, and daily SABA use. Which severity classification best fits, and what is the preferred step of therapy?
AIntermittent — Step 1, SABA as needed
BModerate persistent — Step 3, daily medium-dose ICS (or low-dose ICS-LABA) + SABA prn
CMild persistent — Step 2, daily low-dose ICS + SABA prn
DSevere persistent — Step 4, daily medium-dose ICS-LABA + SABA prn
ENo controller therapy needed
Explanation: Daily symptoms, more-than-weekly (but not nightly) awakenings, some activity limitation, and daily SABA use meet criteria for moderate persistent asthma, whose preferred therapy is daily medium-dose ICS (or low-dose ICS-LABA) with SABA as needed.
Exam-style question
A 13-year-old known asthmatic presents to the office in exacerbation with SpO2 90%, diffuse wheeze, and accessory muscle use, on a viral URI trigger. After the first albuterol nebulizer treatment, her SpO2 transiently drops to 87% before improving. What is the best explanation for this transient desaturation?
ATreatment failure requiring immediate intubation
BA new pneumothorax
CAn allergic reaction to albuterol
DV/Q mismatch from albuterol's vasodilating effect on poorly-ventilated lung units
EWorsening bronchospasm from the nebulizer itself
Explanation: A brief drop in SpO2 immediately after albuterol nebulization is a recognized, usually self-limited phenomenon from V/Q mismatch, as albuterol vasodilates pulmonary vessels supplying poorly-ventilated (and thus poorly-oxygenated) alveolar units.
Exam-style question
A well-controlled 10-year-old asthmatic on a daily controller only develops shortness of breath and wheeze exclusively during soccer practice, which resolves with albuterol taken 15 minutes beforehand. He does not use albuterol at any other time. What is the most appropriate next step?
ANo change needed — continue pre-exercise SABA as his only additional therapy
BStart daily inhaled corticosteroids immediately
CAdd a leukotriene inhibitor with a black box warning discussion
DRefer for immediate spirometry with methacholine challenge
EStart oral prednisone taper
Explanation: Exercise-induced asthma limited strictly to exertion, well controlled with pre-exercise SABA and no SABA use outside of exercise, does not require escalation to daily ICS — that step is reserved for patients using SABA at times unassociated with exercise.

Epidemiology~5.5 million US children with asthma; one of the most common chronic diseases of childhood
Risk factorsParental asthma (2.6x risk); atopy/eczema
Asthma Predictive IndexPositive API (age <3, ≥3 wheeze episodes/yr + parental asthma/eczema, or 2 of allergic rhinitis/non-cold wheeze/eos >4%) → 4-7x increased risk of chronic asthma
Diagnosis by age<5 yrs: no spirometry — trial of meds, reversal with albuterol suggests asthma. ≥5 yrs: spirometry pre/post albuterol is the preferred method
Spirometry obstruction criteriaFEV1 <80% predicted AND FEV1/FVC <85% (0.85)
Significant reversibilityFEV1 increase of >10-12% after bronchodilator
Severity classification axesImpairment (symptom frequency) + Risk (exacerbations/year) → intermittent, mild/moderate/severe persistent
Step therapy backboneStep 1 PRN SABA → Step 2 daily low-dose ICS + PRN SABA → escalating ICS/LABA combinations by age band (0-4, 5-11, 12+), up to daily high-dose ICS-LABA + oral steroid at Step 6
High-yield medication warningMontelukast (leukotriene inhibitor) — black box warning for suicidality/mood disturbance
Exercise-induced asthma treatmentSABA 2 puffs w/spacer 15 min before sport; daily ICS not automatically required unless SABA also used outside of exercise
Asthma Action Plan zonesGreen = doing well (controller meds only); Yellow = worsening (add quick-relief ± oral steroid, call MD); Red = medical alert (quick-relief + oral steroid, call MD/ER now)
Office exacerbation managementBack-to-back albuterol nebulizer x3 with reassessment; consider oral steroid (dexamethasone or prednisone 2mg/kg/day ÷BID x5 days, max 60mg/day); hospitalize if hypoxemic/refractory
Post-albuterol SpO2 dipTransient desaturation from V/Q mismatch is expected and not necessarily treatment failure
Compiled study guide — based on Dr. Jessica Smith's "Not All That Wheezes Is Asthma" and "Asthma Evaluation & Management" lecture series, Rocky Vista University College of Osteopathic Medicine.
